details:
**Langar**
The free communal kitchen found in every gurdwara, where volunteers (sevadars) cook and serve simple vegetarian meals to anyone, regardless of religion, caste, or gender. Diners traditionally sit together on the floor as equals. It is the most frequent clue for Sikhism and usually appears right around the power mark.

**The Five Ks**
The five articles of faith worn at all times by initiated Sikhs: kesh (uncut hair, usually covered by a turban), kangha (a wooden comb), kara (an iron or steel bracelet), kirpan (a curved dagger or sword carried to protect the weak), and kachera (cotton undershorts). The kirpan and kesh are the most commonly mentioned, and the turban is a common giveaway.

**Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth)**
The central scripture of Sikhism, written in the Gurmukhi script and made up of hymns (shabads) by the Sikh Gurus and other saints. Before his death in 1708, the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, declared that the scripture itself would be the eleventh and eternal Guru, so it is treated as a living Guru. It is placed on an elevated throne, and a fan (chaur), traditionally made of yak hair, is waved over it as a sign of respect.

**Mul Mantar and "Ik Onkar"**
The Mul Mantar ("root mantra") is the short opening declaration of the Guru Granth Sahib, which begins the Japji Sahib. Its first words, "Ik Onkar," mean "there is one God" and express Sikhism's strict monotheism. The Ik Onkar symbol is one of the faith's most recognizable emblems.

**Guru Nanak**
The founder and first of the ten human Gurus of Sikhism (1469–1539), born in the Punjab. He is credited with the saying "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim," and his life is told in hagiographies called janamsakhis. One famous janamsakhi story says that when he slept with his feet pointing toward the Kaaba in Mecca and someone turned his feet away, the Kaaba moved to follow them, showing that God is everywhere.

**Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib)**
The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism, located in Amritsar, Punjab, a city founded by the fourth Guru, Ram Das. It sits in a large sacred pool, and its complex also contains the Akal Takht ("Throne of the Timeless One"), the highest seat of temporal authority in Sikhism, established by Guru Hargobind.

**Gurdwara**
The Sikh place of worship, meaning "door to the Guru." Each one houses a copy of the Guru Granth Sahib, contains a langar, and flies the Nishan Sahib, a tall triangular saffron flag bearing the Khanda emblem. The Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Pakistan, where Guru Nanak spent his final years, can be reached from India through the visa-free Kartarpur Corridor.

**Gobind Singh and the Khalsa**
Gobind Singh was the tenth and last human Guru, who founded the Khalsa, the order of fully initiated Sikhs, in 1699, and named the scripture as his successor. Male Khalsa members take the surname Singh ("lion") and women take Kaur ("princess"), and they are described as "saint-soldiers" who combine piety and martial courage. He also wrote the Zafarnama ("Epistle of Victory"), a letter rebuking the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.

**Panj Pyare ("Five Beloved Ones")**
The first five men initiated into the Khalsa. According to tradition, Gobind Singh asked a crowd for a volunteer willing to give his head, took each volunteer into a tent, and came out with a bloody sword, appearing to have beheaded him. In the end he brought all five out alive, and they became the first members of the new order.

**Amrit Sanchar (Khande di Pahul)**
The Sikh initiation ceremony that admits a person to the Khalsa. Amrit, a mixture of water and sugar, is stirred with a double-edged sword called a khanda while prayers are recited; initiates then drink it and have it sprinkled on their eyes and hair. Sikhs who have not undergone the ceremony are called sehajdhari.

**Naam Japo and the Three Pillars**
The three central duties of Sikh life taught by Guru Nanak: Naam Japo (meditating on and repeating the name of God, the Akal Purakh or "Timeless Being"), Kirat Karo (earning an honest living), and Vand Chakko (sharing one's earnings with the community and those in need).

**Five Thieves**
The five vices that Sikhism teaches must be overcome: lust (kaam), anger (krodh), greed (lobh), attachment (moh), and ego or pride (ahankar). They are called thieves because they rob a person of good judgment, and they are subdued through practices such as Naam Japo.

**Karah Prasad**
A sweet, brown pudding made from flour, butter (ghee), and sugar. It is blessed and distributed to everyone in the congregation at the end of a gurdwara service, symbolizing that no one leaves the Guru's presence empty-handed.

**Guru Arjan and Guru Hargobind (Miri-Piri)**
Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, compiled the Adi Granth and was tortured and executed under the Mughals in 1606, including being made to sit on a red-hot iron plate. His son and successor Hargobind responded by wearing two swords representing Miri (temporal power) and Piri (spiritual power), an idea reflected in the two curved swords of the Khanda emblem.

**Naam Karan**
The Sikh naming ceremony for a newborn. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened to a random page, and the first letter of the hymn on that page is used to choose the first letter of the child's name.
